evidence: Traupman 398: molestiam gravem alicui exhibēre, to cause someone big trouble

terms.grammar: phrase: molestus agreeing with the subject, with the dative of the person troubled
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.7.3: nē molestus familiae veniam
Plaut. Men. 627: Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs?
terms.comment: “Stop bothering me!” is comic: Molestus nē sīs! (Plaut. Most. 74, 601; Men. 250), Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs?

terms.gloss: if it’s no trouble, if you don’t mind
terms.grammar: phrase, with a request (velim and the subjunctive)
evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.46: nisi molestum est, … velim scīre
Cic. Acad. 1.14: renovārī ā tē, nisi molestum est, velim
terms.comment: Also ubi molestum nōn erit, when it’s no trouble (Ter. Eun. 483); Traupman (p. 110) gives sī grave nōn erit. Without any trouble: nūllō negōtiō (see problem).

phrases.latin: sed tamen, nisi molestum est, ex tribus istīs modīs rērum pūblicārum velim scīre quod optimum jūdicēs
phrases.english: but still, if it’s no trouble, I should like to know which of those three kinds of state you think best

phrases.latin: nōlō eō diē in Albānum venīre, nē molestus familiae veniam
phrases.english: I don’t want to come to the Alban villa on that day, so as not to be a nuisance to the household

phrases.latin: Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs? num tē appellō?
phrases.english: Can’t you stop bothering me? I’m not talking to you, am I?

sources: Lewis & Short: molestia · Lewis & Short: molestus
